title: The Argyll Robertson Pupil: A Clinical Masterclass
summary: The Argyll Robertson Pupil (ARP) represents a hallmark neuro-ophthalmological sign of neurosyphilis, characterized by light-near dissociation. This poster provides a high-yield synthesis for clinicians, bridging pathophysiology with modern diagnostic excellence.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Argyll Robertson Pupil (ARP) is classically defined by 'light-near dissociation' (LND). The pupils exhibit: 1) Failure to constrict to direct light, 2) Preservation of constriction during accommodation, 3) Miosis, and 4) Poor dilation in response to mydriatics due to iris atrophy/fibrosis.

rows: Lesions in the pretectal nuclei of the midbrain
Disruption of the light reflex arc; sparing of the accommodation-convergence pathway
Historically associated with chronic untreated Treponema pallidum infection

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Worry
content: Presence of optic atrophy or severe vision loss (requires rule-out of syphilitic optic neuropathy)
Complete lack of iris movement (consider mechanical synechiae)

sections.title: Clinical Diagnostic Workup
content: Step 1: Slit-lamp exam to evaluate for iris atrophy and synechiae.
Step 2: Compare reaction to light vs. near stimulus (e.g., accommodative target).
Step 4: Lumbar puncture for CSF VDRL and protein/cell count analysis.

content.explanation: A: Accommodation present; R: Reflex (light) absent; P: Pupil small (miotic).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: The pupils are often irregular and asymmetric, not just small.
They show poor dilation to hydroxyamphetamine because the postganglionic sympathetic fibers are typically intact in pure neurosyphilis.
Always perform a full neurological exam for signs of Tabes Dorsalis (loss of proprioception/vibration).
Even with modern antibiotics, clinicians must maintain a high index of suspicion in immunocompromised populations.
